a: Content is sent to you before publishing, so you stay in control of what goes out under your name. Review processes are agreed during onboarding.
t: Clear packages. Honest starting prices.

q: What is the difference between Launch and Growth?
a: Launch covers 4 posts a month, basic local SEO and a monthly report. Growth doubles content to 8 posts a month, includes fuller SEO, and adds tracking set-up and regular review.
t: Clear packages. Honest starting prices.

q: Can I embed my class booking system on my website?
a: Most class booking systems offer a way to embed a timetable or link to a booking page. The design should make that step feel consistent with the rest of the site, and it should work well on mobile.
t: Yoga and Pilates Studio Website Design: Timetables, Classes and Memberships

q: Should a yoga studio website list prices?
a: Generally yes. Clear prices for drop-ins, class packs and memberships help people decide, and terms such as expiry and notice periods should be visible before payment.
t: Yoga and Pilates Studio Website Design: Timetables, Classes and Memberships

q: How can a studio website help beginners?
a: A new students page explaining which classes to start with, what to bring and what to expect, along with clear level labels on the timetable, can help beginners feel confident booking.
t: Yoga and Pilates Studio Website Design: Timetables, Classes and Memberships

q: Can yoga studios make health claims on their website?
a: Describe classes accurately but avoid promising specific health outcomes. Advertising rules apply to website claims, and health claims need to be supportable.
t: Yoga and Pilates Studio Website Design: Timetables, Classes and Memberships

q: Do reformer Pilates studios need different booking features?
a: Reformer classes usually have a fixed number of machines, so booking needs to handle limited capacity, waitlists and late cancellations reliably.
t: Yoga and Pilates Studio Website Design: Timetables, Classes and Memberships

q: Why can I not find the Widgets menu in WordPress?
a: If your site uses a block theme, there is no Widgets menu, because widget areas are replaced by templates and template parts edited in the Site Editor. With a classic theme, the menu sits under Appearance, though some themes have no widget areas at all.
t: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars: How to Use Them Well

q: Can I use blocks in widget areas?
a: Yes. In recent versions of WordPress, the widgets screen in classic themes is block-based, so you can add standard blocks such as paragraphs, images and buttons to widget areas.
t: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars: How to Use Them Well

q: Do sidebars help SEO?
a: A sidebar is not an SEO feature in itself. Sensible internal links in a sidebar can help visitors and search engines discover related content, but a cluttered sidebar full of links adds little. Focus on usefulness to visitors first.
t: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars: How to Use Them Well

q: Will changing my theme delete my widgets?
a: Changing theme does not usually delete widget content outright, but widgets may be moved to an inactive area or placed in different locations because the new theme has different widget areas. Check and rearrange them after any theme change, ideally on a staging copy first.
t: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars: How to Use Them Well

q: Should my homepage have a sidebar?
a: Often not. Homepages tend to work better with a focused, full-width layout that guides visitors towards your main services or products. Sidebars are more commonly useful on blog posts and archive pages.
t: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars: How to Use Them Well

q: How many Administrators should a WordPress site have?
a: As few as practical. Usually the business owner and whoever maintains the site technically. Everyone else should have a lower role suited to their work.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: What is the difference between an Editor and an Author?
a: An Editor can publish and edit everyone's posts and pages. An Author can only publish and edit their own posts.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: Is it safe to share one login between staff?
a: It is not recommended. Shared logins make it impossible to see who changed what and hard to remove one person's access. Give each person their own account.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: What happens to posts when I delete a user?
a: WordPress asks whether to delete their content or attribute it to another user. Choose to attribute it to another account unless you genuinely want the content removed.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: Can I create my own user roles?
a: Yes, with a role management plugin or custom code. Keep changes minimal, document them and test with a dummy account first.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: Can Prism Works Studio review our WordPress access?
a: Yes. Prism Works Studio can review your user accounts and roles and recommend a safer setup as part of our website and ecommerce development work.
t: WordPress User Roles: How to Give the Right People the Right Access

q: How long do items stay in the WordPress trash?
a: WordPress removes trashed items automatically after a default period, which developers can change. If you need something back, restore it as soon as you notice it is missing.
t: WordPress Trash: How to Restore Deleted Pages, Posts and Media

q: Why did my restored page come back as a draft?
a: Recent versions of WordPress restore trashed content as a draft so you can review it before it goes live again. Check the content and publish it when ready.
t: WordPress Trash: How to Restore Deleted Pages, Posts and Media

q: Can I recover an image I deleted from the media library?
a: Media deletions are usually permanent by default. The main options are restoring from a backup or re-uploading the original file.
t: WordPress Trash: How to Restore Deleted Pages, Posts and Media

q: Does deleting a page affect my search rankings?
a: It can, if the page received visits from search or links from other sites. Restoring it quickly, or redirecting it to a relevant alternative, helps reduce the impact.
t: WordPress Trash: How to Restore Deleted Pages, Posts and Media

q: Who can delete content in WordPress?
a: It depends on user roles. Administrators and editors can usually delete most content, while authors and contributors have more limited permissions over their own work.
t: WordPress Trash: How to Restore Deleted Pages, Posts and Media

q: What is the difference between a synced and an unsynced pattern?
a: A synced pattern stays linked everywhere it is used, so editing it updates every copy. An unsynced pattern inserts independent copies of its blocks, which can each be edited without affecting the original or other copies.
t: WordPress Synced Patterns: How to Reuse Content Without Copying It

q: What happened to reusable blocks in WordPress?
a: Reusable blocks were renamed and became synced patterns. They work in a similar way, and existing reusable blocks on older sites should appear among your patterns.
t: WordPress Synced Patterns: How to Reuse Content Without Copying It

q: Can I change a synced pattern on just one page?
a: You can detach the pattern on that page, which turns it into regular blocks you can edit freely. That copy will no longer receive future updates. Some recent WordPress versions also allow selected parts of a synced pattern to be overridden per page, depending on your setup.
t: WordPress Synced Patterns: How to Reuse Content Without Copying It

q: Do patterns work with classic themes?
a: Patterns are a block editor feature, so they are available wherever you use the block editor for posts and pages, including on sites with classic themes. Managing patterns through the Site Editor applies to block themes.
t: WordPress Synced Patterns: How to Reuse Content Without Copying It

q: Will deleting a synced pattern remove it from my pages?
a: Deleting a synced pattern that is still in use can leave affected pages with missing content or an error message in its place. Check where a pattern is used, and replace or detach those instances, before deleting it.
t: WordPress Synced Patterns: How to Reuse Content Without Copying It

q: Where is Site Health in WordPress?
a: Go to Tools, then Site Health, in the WordPress dashboard. You need an administrator account to see it.
t: WordPress Site Health Screen: How to Read It and What to Do About It

q: Do I need to fix every Site Health recommendation?
a: Not always. Critical issues deserve prompt attention, while recommended improvements can be weighed up and planned into maintenance. Some may not apply to your setup.
t: WordPress Site Health Screen: How to Read It and What to Do About It

q: Is it safe to upgrade PHP when Site Health suggests it?
a: It is usually worthwhile, but check that your theme and extensions support the newer version, take a backup and test on staging first.
t: WordPress Site Health Screen: How to Read It and What to Do About It

q: Does Site Health check for malware?
a: No. It checks configuration and settings, but it does not scan for malware or confirm that a site is clean.
t: WordPress Site Health Screen: How to Read It and What to Do About It

q: Should I share my Site Health info with a developer?
a: It can speed up troubleshooting. Read it first, as it includes server details, and share it only with people you trust.
t: WordPress Site Health Screen: How to Read It and What to Do About It

q: What is the difference between a template and a template part?
a: A template is the full layout for a type of page. A template part is a section, such as a header or footer, that can be reused inside several templates.
t: WordPress Site Editor Templates and Template Parts: A Practical Guide

q: Is a synced pattern the same as a template part?
a: They behave similarly because both update everywhere when edited, but synced patterns are designed for content inside pages, while template parts are part of the site's layout structure.
t: WordPress Site Editor Templates and Template Parts: A Practical Guide

q: Will editing a template change every page?
a: It changes every page that uses that template. Check which template a page uses before editing, and test larger changes on a staging site.
t: WordPress Site Editor Templates and Template Parts: A Practical Guide

q: Can I undo changes to a template?
a: In most cases you can reset a customised template to the theme's original version, but this removes your edits. Keep a backup and a note of changes before making large adjustments.
t: WordPress Site Editor Templates and Template Parts: A Practical Guide

q: Does my site use the site editor?
a: Only if it uses a block theme. Classic themes manage layout differently, usually through theme files, the customiser and widgets.
t: WordPress Site Editor Templates and Template Parts: A Practical Guide

q: Do global styles work with classic themes?
a: No. The Styles panel is part of the Site Editor, which is available with block themes. Classic themes use the Customizer or their own settings instead.
t: WordPress Site Editor Styles: Managing Global Fonts and Colours

q: Will updating my theme remove my style changes?
a: Changes made in the Styles panel are stored separately in the database, so a theme update should not remove them. Theme defaults you have not customised may change, so review the site after updates.
t: WordPress Site Editor Styles: Managing Global Fonts and Colours

q: Can I upload my brand font?
a: Recent WordPress versions let you upload font files through the font library. Check that your font licence allows web use first.
t: WordPress Site Editor Styles: Managing Global Fonts and Colours

q: How do I undo a style change?
a: Use the revision history in the Styles panel to restore an earlier version, or reset to theme defaults if you want to start again.
t: WordPress Site Editor Styles: Managing Global Fonts and Colours

q: Should editors be able to pick any colour?
a: Usually not. Restricting choices to a brand palette keeps the site consistent and helps make sure colour combinations remain readable.
t: WordPress Site Editor Styles: Managing Global Fonts and Colours

q: Does WordPress have built-in search?
a: Yes. WordPress includes a basic search that looks at the titles, content and excerpts of published posts and pages, displayed using your theme's search template.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: Can I edit the search results page without code?
a: On a block theme, you can edit the search results template in the site editor. On a classic theme, changes usually need a developer working in a child theme.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: Should search results pages be indexed by Google?
a: Generally not. Internal search pages can create many thin pages, so many sites set them to noindex. Check how your setup handles this.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: How do I remove certain pages from search results?
a: This normally involves adjusting the search query or using settings in your search setup. Ask your developer to make the change and test it.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: What should the no results page say?
a: Repeat the search term, suggest alternative searches, show the search box again and link to key pages and your contact details.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: How can I see what visitors search for?
a: Many analytics setups can record site search terms. Once enabled, review them regularly for patterns and gaps.
t: WordPress Search Results Page: Helping Visitors Find What They Need

q: Why does my scheduled post say "Missed schedule"?
a: WordPress did not run its publishing task at the scheduled time. Common reasons include a timezone mismatch, caching, the task runner being disabled without a replacement, or the server blocking the site's internal request. Publish it manually, then look for the cause.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Which timezone should a UK WordPress site use?
a: Choose London from the city list in Settings, then General. A fixed UTC offset does not follow the clock changes, so scheduled times will be an hour out for part of the year.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Can I schedule pages as well as posts?
a: Yes. Pages, and most custom post types that use the standard editor, have the same publish date option.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Does a scheduled post publish at the exact minute?
a: Not always. With the default setup it publishes on the first visit after the scheduled time. A server task that runs at a fixed interval makes timing more predictable.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Will scheduling posts improve my SEO?
a: No, scheduling is a workflow tool. It can help you publish consistently, but rankings depend on the quality and usefulness of the content, not on when it was scheduled.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Can I bulk reschedule posts?
a: The standard quick edit option lets you change dates on posts one at a time from the posts list. For larger changes, plan carefully and test on a staging copy first.
t: WordPress Scheduled Posts: Scheduling, Timezones and Fixing Missed Schedules

q: Where are WordPress revisions stored?
a: Revisions are stored in your site's database as special entries linked to the original post. They are not visible to visitors and do not create separate pages on your site.
t: WordPress Revisions and Autosave: How to Recover and Compare Content

q: Do revisions slow down my website?
a: Revisions are not loaded when visitors view your pages, so they do not usually affect front-end speed directly. A very large number of stored revisions can make the database bigger, which is one reason some sites choose to limit them.
t: WordPress Revisions and Autosave: How to Recover and Compare Content

q: Can I recover a deleted post?
a: Posts moved to the Bin can be restored from there until the Bin is emptied. Once a post is permanently deleted, its revisions go with it, and you would need to restore from a backup.
t: WordPress Revisions and Autosave: How to Recover and Compare Content

q: Why does my page not have any revisions?
a: It may have only been saved once, revisions may be disabled on your site, or the content type may not support them. Your developer or hosting provider can check the configuration.
t: WordPress Revisions and Autosave: How to Recover and Compare Content

q: Does autosave publish my changes?
a: No. On a published post, autosave stores your changes separately and does not alter the live page until you choose to update.
t: WordPress Revisions and Autosave: How to Recover and Compare Content

q: Why is my WordPress site not showing in Google?
a: There can be many reasons, but check the search engine visibility box in Settings, then Reading first. If it is ticked, search engines are being asked not to index the site.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: Why does my blog page ignore the content I added?
a: When a page is set as the posts page, WordPress fills it with your post list and most themes ignore the page's own content. Put introductory text in the theme's archive settings or template instead.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: Should I turn off comments on my business blog?
a: If nobody has time to moderate and reply, turning them off is often better than leaving comments unanswered. You can still invite questions through a contact form.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: Do Discussion settings change existing posts?
a: The default post settings only apply to new posts. Use bulk edit in the posts list to open or close comments on existing posts.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: What are pingbacks and trackbacks?
a: They are notices one site sends to another when it links to it. They are rarely useful for business sites and often attract spam, so many owners switch them off.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: Is the search visibility setting enough to hide a staging site?
a: No. It is a request to search engines, not access control. Use password protection or your host's privacy tools as well.
t: WordPress Reading and Discussion Settings: What Each Option Does

q: How many plugins is too many for WordPress?
a: There is no magic number. What matters is whether each plugin is needed, maintained and well built. A few poorly made plugins can cause more trouble than many good ones.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: Is it safe to delete inactive plugins?
a: Usually yes, if you are sure they are not needed. Take a backup first and check whether the plugin stores data you want to keep.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: How do I know if a plugin is abandoned?
a: Check its last update date and whether it is marked as tested with recent WordPress versions. Long gaps without updates suggest it may no longer be maintained.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: Can removing a plugin break my site?
a: It can, if something depends on it. That is why you should back up, test on staging and remove plugins one at a time.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: Do plugins slow WordPress down?
a: Some do, particularly those that load scripts on every page. Removing unnecessary plugins is often one of the simpler ways to lighten a site.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: Can Prism Works Studio audit my plugins?
a: Yes. We can review your WordPress site and talk through what to keep, replace or remove. Get in touch via our contact page.
t: WordPress Plugin Audit: How to Review, Remove and Replace Plugins

q: What is the best permalink structure for WordPress?
a: There is no single best option, but the post name structure is a sensible default for many business sites because it is short and readable. News-style sites may prefer a date-based structure.
t: WordPress Permalink Settings: How to Choose and Change Your URL Structure

q: Is it safe to change permalinks in WordPress?
a: On a new site it is low risk. On an established site it changes URLs, so back up first, test on staging and set up redirects from old URLs to new ones.
t: WordPress Permalink Settings: How to Choose and Change Your URL Structure

q: Why are my WordPress pages showing not found after a change?
a: The rewrite rules may need refreshing. Visiting Settings, then Permalinks, and saving without changes often fixes it.
t: WordPress Permalink Settings: How to Choose and Change Your URL Structure

q: Should I include the category in WordPress URLs?
a: It can add context, but if you reorganise categories later the URLs will change. A simpler structure is less fragile if your categories are still evolving.
t: WordPress Permalink Settings: How to Choose and Change Your URL Structure

q: Can I change the slug of a single post?
a: Yes, in the post settings panel of the editor. If the post is already live, add a redirect from the old URL to the new one.
t: WordPress Permalink Settings: How to Choose and Change Your URL Structure

q: Is WordPress Multisite free?
a: Yes, Multisite is a built-in feature of WordPress. You will still need suitable hosting, and some premium plugins license network use differently, so check their terms.
t: WordPress Multisite Explained: Pros, Cons and Alternatives

q: Can each Multisite site have its own domain name?
a: Yes. Current versions of WordPress support mapping custom domains to individual sites in a network, subject to your hosting and DNS setup.
t: WordPress Multisite Explained: Pros, Cons and Alternatives

q: Can each site use different plugins?
a: Plugins are installed once for the network, but the Super Admin can allow individual sites to activate them separately, so sites can use different combinations.
t: WordPress Multisite Explained: Pros, Cons and Alternatives

q: Is Multisite less secure than separate sites?
a: Not inherently, but a vulnerability or fault can affect every site at once. Strong security practice and careful update testing are especially important.
t: WordPress Multisite Explained: Pros, Cons and Alternatives

q: Can I run WooCommerce on Multisite?
a: WooCommerce can run on a Multisite network, with each site acting as a separate store. Check compatibility of any extensions you rely on before committing.
t: WordPress Multisite Explained: Pros, Cons and Alternatives

q: Why can I not find the Menus option in WordPress?
a: If Appearance does not show a Menus option, your site is most likely using a block theme. In that case, menus are managed through the Navigation block in the Site Editor instead.
t: WordPress Menus: A Practical Guide to Building Site Navigation

q: Can I have different menus on different pages?
a: Yes, though how you do it depends on your theme. Block themes let you use different template parts with different Navigation blocks. Classic themes may need theme options or custom development to show different menus on specific pages.
t: WordPress Menus: A Practical Guide to Building Site Navigation

q: How many items should a main menu have?
a: There is no fixed number. Aim for a menu visitors can scan quickly, focused on the main things they come to your site for, and move secondary links elsewhere.
t: WordPress Menus: A Practical Guide to Building Site Navigation

q: Does the menu affect SEO?
a: Menus help search engines discover and understand your important pages, because they are linked from every page. Clear, descriptive labels and a sensible structure help both visitors and search engines.
t: WordPress Menus: A Practical Guide to Building Site Navigation

q: Will changing my menu break anything?
a: Changing menu items does not change page addresses, so it should not break links elsewhere. However, removing a page from the menu can make it harder to find, so make sure important content is still linked from somewhere.
t: WordPress Menus: A Practical Guide to Building Site Navigation

q: Can I create folders in the WordPress media library?
a: Not by default. WordPress organises uploads by date behind the scenes. Folders can be added with a media organisation tool if your library is large.
t: WordPress Media Library Organisation: A Practical Guide

q: Is it safe to delete unused images?
a: It can be, but check carefully first. Images may be used in places WordPress does not track, so back up and test before deleting.
t: WordPress Media Library Organisation: A Practical Guide

q: Does the file name of an image matter for SEO?
a: A descriptive file name, along with good alt text, helps search engines understand an image. It is a small but worthwhile habit.
t: WordPress Media Library Organisation: A Practical Guide

q: What should alt text say?
a: Describe what the image shows and why it is on the page, briefly and naturally. Decorative images can have empty alt text.
t: WordPress Media Library Organisation: A Practical Guide

q: Why are there so many copies of each image?
a: WordPress creates resized versions of each uploaded image for different parts of your theme. This is normal behaviour.
t: WordPress Media Library Organisation: A Practical Guide

q: What size should I upload images to WordPress?
a: It depends on the largest space the image appears in on your theme. Resize to suit that space, allowing for high-density screens, rather than uploading full camera files.
t: WordPress Image Sizes and Thumbnails: How to Get Them Right

q: What is the difference between a featured image and a thumbnail?
a: A featured image is the main image chosen for a post. WordPress calls it a post thumbnail in code, and themes display it in various sizes, including the small thumbnail size.
t: WordPress Image Sizes and Thumbnails: How to Get Them Right

q: Why do my old images look wrong after changing theme?
a: Existing images keep the sizes created when they were uploaded. Regenerating image sizes creates new copies that match the new theme.
t: WordPress Image Sizes and Thumbnails: How to Get Them Right

q: Can I stop WordPress creating so many image sizes?
a: Some sizes can be changed or disabled, but themes may rely on them. Check what your theme uses before removing any sizes, ideally with developer help.
t: WordPress Image Sizes and Thumbnails: How to Get Them Right

q: Does WordPress compress images automatically?
a: WordPress applies some compression to resized copies, but compressing images before upload usually gives you more control over quality and file size.
t: WordPress Image Sizes and Thumbnails: How to Get Them Right

q: Is it safe to clean a WordPress database?
a: It can be, provided you take a full tested backup first and stick to well-understood tasks such as removing spam, trash and expired transients. Deleting tables or options needs more care.
t: WordPress Database Cleanup: How to Tidy Up Safely

q: Should I delete all post revisions?
a: Not necessarily. Revisions let you roll back changes. Many site owners keep a few recent revisions per page and remove older ones.
t: WordPress Database Cleanup: How to Tidy Up Safely

q: Do deleted plugins leave data behind?
a: They can. Some plugins remove their data on uninstall, while others leave tables and options in place unless you remove them separately.
t: WordPress Database Cleanup: How to Tidy Up Safely

q: Will cleaning my database improve SEO?
a: Not directly. It may help performance in some cases, which supports a good visitor experience, but content, structure and technical health matter far more for search.
t: WordPress Database Cleanup: How to Tidy Up Safely

q: Can I clean a WooCommerce store database?
a: Yes, with extra caution. Order and customer data may be needed for accounts and customer service, so check what you need to keep before removing anything.
t: WordPress Database Cleanup: How to Tidy Up Safely

q: Do I need a developer to create custom post types?
a: Not necessarily. Plugins can create them through a settings screen. A developer is useful when you need custom templates, complex fields or a clean, plugin-light setup.
t: WordPress Custom Post Types: When and How to Use Them

q: Will I lose content if I remove a custom post type?
a: Unregistering a post type hides it, but the content generally remains in the database. Registering it again with the same name usually brings it back. Always take a backup before making structural changes.
t: WordPress Custom Post Types: When and How to Use Them

q: Can custom post types use the block editor?
a: Yes, provided the post type is registered with REST API support and the editor feature enabled. Without that, WordPress falls back to the classic editing screen.
t: WordPress Custom Post Types: When and How to Use Them

q: What is the difference between a custom post type and a custom field?
a: A custom post type is a new kind of content, such as Projects. Custom fields are individual pieces of information attached to content, such as a project's location or completion photos.
t: WordPress Custom Post Types: When and How to Use Them

q: Are custom post types good for SEO?
a: They are neutral in themselves. They can help by giving content clear structure, logical URLs and dedicated templates, but the quality of the content still matters most.
t: WordPress Custom Post Types: When and How to Use Them

q: How do I stop spam comments in WordPress?
a: Use the discussion settings to require approval and hold comments with links, add spam filtering if comments are active, or switch comments off if you do not need them.
t: WordPress Comment Spam: How to Reduce It and Manage Comments

q: Should a business website allow comments?
a: It depends. If readers genuinely use comments to ask questions, they can be valuable. If not, switching them off saves time and removes a spam route.
t: WordPress Comment Spam: How to Reduce It and Manage Comments

q: What are trackbacks and pingbacks?
a: They are notifications sent when another site links to your content. They are frequently abused by spammers, and many sites switch them off.
t: WordPress Comment Spam: How to Reduce It and Manage Comments

q: Does comment spam affect SEO?
a: Published spam with low-quality links can make a page look poorly maintained. Keeping spam unpublished avoids that risk.
t: WordPress Comment Spam: How to Reduce It and Manage Comments

q: Should I delete spam comments?
a: Yes, periodically. Check for genuine comments caught by mistake, then empty the spam folder to keep your database tidy.
t: WordPress Comment Spam: How to Reduce It and Manage Comments

q: Will a child theme slow my site down?
a: A properly built child theme adds very little overhead, because it mostly reuses the parent's files. Speed problems usually come from heavy themes, plugins or images rather than the child theme itself.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: Can I add a child theme to an existing site?
a: Yes. You can create and activate a child theme at any point. Test on staging first, because classic themes may need menus or widgets reassigned after switching.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: What if my parent theme was edited directly?
a: Identify the changes, ideally by comparing the edited files with a fresh copy of the same theme version, then move them into a child theme or a custom plugin before updating the parent.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: Do block themes still need child themes?
a: Not always. Many changes can be made in the Site Editor. A child block theme is useful when you want templates and settings stored as files that can be tracked and deployed.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: Should custom functionality go in the child theme?
a: Only if it is genuinely part of the design. Features you would want to keep after changing theme, such as custom post types, usually belong in a plugin.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: Can Prism Works Studio set up or clean up a child theme?
a: Yes. Prism Works Studio can audit theme changes, move customisations into a child theme or plugin and test updates as part of our website and ecommerce development work.
t: WordPress Child Themes: When You Need One and How to Use It Safely

q: Should I use categories or tags?
a: Use categories for every post to define its main section. Tags are optional and best used for specific details shared by several posts.
t: WordPress Categories and Tags: Organising Your Blog for Readers and Search

q: How many categories should a blog have?
a: There is no fixed number. Aim for a small set of distinct topics that you will write about regularly.
t: WordPress Categories and Tags: Organising Your Blog for Readers and Search

q: Can a post have more than one category?
a: Yes, but giving each post one main category usually keeps the structure clearer.
t: WordPress Categories and Tags: Organising Your Blog for Readers and Search

q: Are tag pages bad for SEO?
a: Not in themselves, but many thin tag pages with only one or two posts can add little value. Keep tags purposeful and consider your indexing settings.
t: WordPress Categories and Tags: Organising Your Blog for Readers and Search

q: What happens to posts if I delete a category?
